chunks: And from him, from Ali, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"The divorced woman observes her waiting period in her house, and it is not appropriate for her to go out until her waiting period is completed. Her waiting period is three menstrual periods or three months, unless she is menstruating."

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And if she is one of those who do not menstruate, but similar women do, her waiting period is three months. And if she has despaired of menstruation, and similar women do not menstruate, then there is no waiting period upon her, and the limit of that is fifty years, and its maximum is sixty years.

This is indicated by what we have previously mentioned of the narrations, and it is also indicated by His Exalted saying: "And those of you who die and leave wives — they should be bequeathed for their wives a year's maintenance? No, rather, those who despair of menstruation among your women, if you have doubt, then their waiting period is three months, and [also for] those who have not menstruated."
So He obligated upon one who does not menstruate, if she is in doubt, a waiting period of three months.
ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for a divorced woman according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the hadith by establishing a scholarly consensus on the age thresholds for menopause, defining the onset at fifty years and the absolute limit at sixty, which determines the applicability of the three-month waiting period for post-menopausal women. This legal nuance ensures that the ruling for 'al-lati yasi'na' (those who have ceased menstruating) is applied precisely based on physiological certainty rather than mere assumption, reinforcing the practical application of Quranic injunctions in Shia jurisprudence.
